title: Emit ripple analysis and microqueue logbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working log of an exploratory investigation into a recurring pattern we observed in production traces that I’m calling an "emit ripple" — a small, early-delay in token emission that propagates downstream, causing microqueue build ups and P95/P99 spikes for short-to-medium length sequences. The goal is to capture sampling methodology, representative traces, quant breakdowns, hypotheses, and lightweight mitigations to test in the canary pool.

Background / why I started this:
- Starting mid-Oct we saw periodic P95 regressions on the conversational route despite p50 being stable.
- Existing SLO dashboards pointed at increased stage variance around the emitter/egress boundary but didn’t explain root cause.
- Hypothesis: intermittent micro-delays (10–40ms) in emit/egress cause downstream batcher handoffs to miss favorable batching windows -> extra batching_wait for subsequent requests, cascading into p95 spikes for short responses.

Data and sampling method:
- Trace corpus: 18k end-to-end traces sampled over 72 hours (prod-west-1, peak/off-peak mix).
- Sampling strata: by seqlen (<=16, 17–64, 65–256), kv_cache (hit/miss/partial), route-tag (chat/complete/embeddings) -> focused on chat and complete for this work.
- Instrumentation: per-stage timestamps (client_recv, tokenization, model_infer_start, kv_lookup, batch_wait_enter/exit, emit_first_token, emit_last_token, egress_submit).
- Synthetic replays: 2 controlled replays against canary fleet with 2000 traces each, toggling pacer max_wait_ms and early-flush heuristics.

Representative aggregate numbers (selected cohorts):
- Cohort A (seqlen <=16, kv_cache hit): p50=45ms, p95=120ms, p99=210ms
- Cohort B (seqlen 17-64, kv_cache miss): p50=120ms, p95=420ms, p99=780ms
- Cohort C (seqlen <=16, kv_cache miss): p50=65ms, p95=330ms, p99=610ms

Per-stage median breakdown (Cohort A typical fast trace):
- tokenization: 4ms
- model_infer (first pass): 18ms
- batch_wait: 8ms
- kv_lookup: 1ms
- emit (first token latency): 6ms
- egress_submit+net: 8ms
(total ~45ms p50)

Per-stage tail contributors (Cohort A p95/p99):
- emit-first-token jitter (10–60ms) — often correlated with CPU scheduler preemption on the emitter thread
- batch_wait late wakeups (25–90ms) — when a wake-up aligns just after the small emission ripple window
- small number of kv_lookup stalls (lock contention) adding 20–120ms in some p99 paths

Key patterns observed in trace-level timelines:
- Pattern 1: "micro-ripple cascade" — a short delay on trace N emit (10–40ms) coincides with a batcher flush boundary such that trace N+1 arrives just after flush, pushing it to wait for the next batch window (additional 30–70ms). The net effect: N shows slightly higher emit latency, N+1 shows elevated batch_wait.
- Pattern 2: "emit jitter clusters" — multiple requests in a tight cohort where one worker hits an OS preemption or GC pause, creating a clustered tail for 3–6 traces in that micro-epoch.
- Pattern 3: "kv-lock spikes" — rare but visible when shared kv cache maintenance (eviction) runs concurrently, causing 50–200ms stalls.

Quick correlation stats (from sample):
- fraction of p95 traces where batch_wait contributed >30% of end-to-end: 42%
- fraction where emit-first-token jitter >25ms: 36%
- cohort overlap where both occurred: 18%

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Scheduling jitter on emitter threads combined with tight batching windows produces the ripple effect (primary).
2) Batcher wake policy too brittle for mixed seqlen traffic — short live sequences lose out when they narrowly miss a flush.
3) KV cache maintenance occasionally introduces stalls that amplify the ripple into a multi-trace tail.

Proof-of-concept mitigations tested in synthetic replay (results below):
- A: Decrease pacer.max_wait_ms from 30ms -> 15ms (aggressive early flush): p95 drop for Cohort A from 120ms -> 95ms, p99 from 210ms -> 180ms, but CPU utilization up ~6% and token cost +1.8%.
- B: Introduce emitter-thread CPU affinity (dedicated soft affinity for emitter) on canary nodes: reduced emit-first-token jitter frequency by ~28%, p95 improvement ~12%.
- C: Add adaptive early-flush for cohorts with seqlen<=16 and kv_cache hit: similar p95 gains to A but with less CPU overhead (cost +0.7%).

Trade-offs and caveats:
- Lowering max_wait reduces the ripple but increases flush frequency -> higher GPU utilization (smaller micro-batches have worse per-token efficiency). Need to quantify unit-cost impact across traffic mix.
- Emitter affinity helps but is brittle across noisy host environments; requires coordination with node packing and other services.
- KV lock work suggests we should split maintenance jobs away from hot path threads (further infra work).

Concrete next steps (short list):
- Short (<2 week) experiments: roll adaptive early-flush to 10% canary traffic for 24–48h and compare p50/p95/p99 and unit cost by route.
- Mid (2–6 weeks): prototype lightweight emitter CPU QoS policy on canary fleet and instrument thread-level preemption metrics.
- Infra: schedule a follow-up to move kv maintenance off hot path (owned by infra team) and add lock-free read paths for hot-key hits.
- Observability: add a new microqueue backpressure metric and a small dashboard showing emit-first-token jitter distribution correlated with batcher flush offsets.

Notable sample traces (IDs from the corpus) for replay/triage:
- trace-20241106-west-00712 (micro-ripple cascade; seqlen=12; kv=hit)
- trace-20241109-west-01599 (emit jitter cluster; 4 traces back-to-back)
- trace-20241112-west-00301 (kv-lock spike; p99 path)

Open questions / things to watch:
- Does adaptive flush create oscillations under sudden load shifts? (need synthetic burst tests)
- Is emitter jitter correlated with specific host kernels or container runtimes? (ask infra for host-level audit)
- Can we detect micro-ripple in real time and do adaptive client-side backpressure instead of server-only fixes?

Notes to self / quick todo checklist:
- [ ] Push canary config for adaptive-early-flush (PR linked)
- [ ] Add microqueue metric to telemetry proto (small schema change)
- [ ] Trigger infra ticket for kv maintenance isolation (JIRA: JIRA-RT-3301)
- [ ] Run bursty synthetic traffic with mixed seqlen for 3 hours and capture traces

Appendix - quick replay script pointers:
- replay command used on canary: ./tools/trace_replay --corpus traces/emit-ripple-sample.json --rate 250/s --canary true --pacer-policy adaptive-earlyflush
- PR for adaptive policy: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1458

If useful I can convert key charts (p50/p95/p99 by cohort and per-stage stacked bars) into a short slide deck for the weekly SRE sync. For now keeping this as a working log — will update after the 10% canary run.

-- Aisha (field notes)
